lines.text: A customer asks for a refund on a forty-nine dollar order. The payment goes through, but the reply is slow.
After one second, the agent gives up and tries again. Ninety-eight dollars, refunded on a forty-nine dollar order.
No crash. No failing test. Under real-world failures, this agent keeps its rules only fifty-six percent of the time.
And every other approach waits for it to break, then heals it.
It's chaos engineering for AI agents. It attacks your agent before your users do, writes the fix, and only accepts it when an independent Judge proves it.
Red reads the code, finds the weak links, and attacks them in a sandbox. Timeouts. Rate limits. Prompt injection. A customer who claims to be the CEO.
Blue writes a fix. The Judge re-runs every attack, on seeds Blue never saw. The first fix still pays twice. Rejected. Rolled back to a checkpoint.
The next adds an idempotency key, but three tickets get no reply. Rejected again. The third passes fifty-nine out of fifty-nine, enough to prove a ninety-five percent target.
Same seed, before and after. The second refund is gone.
Fifty-six percent, to one hundred. Five hundred fifty-three thousand dollars at risk per thousand tickets, down to zero. And a pull request, with tests proven to catch the bug.
Every run is a neatlogs session, one trace per phase, and Blue reads failing traces back before it writes a fix.
Entire names the AI session that wrote the bug. And the business plan is built in cfo.ai.
It isn't tied to one agent. ResearchBot, on real Crustdata data: forty-nine to one hundred. Several faults at once: forty-three to one hundred.
Bulwark even attacks itself. Eleven faults, eleven recovered.
Bulwark. Break it first. Agents you can trust to run without you watching.
